transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-01-28
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~47 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Patel (Redwood AE), Carlos Mendes (Redwood SE), Jared Kim (AeroFin - Head of ML), Priya Desai (AeroFin - Infra Lead), Mark Liao (AeroFin - CTO)

Summary (auto): Short discovery to understand AeroFin's inference needs and evaluate Dedicated reserved capacity vs Hosted/Private. Focus on reserved GPU sizes, isolation, burst strategy, scaling expectations, and security requirements. Next steps: share pricing, benchmark plan, schedule PoC.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros, I'm Sofia, account exec on Redwood, and Carlos is our solutions engineer.
[00:08] Carlos: hey all, hi, um, hi Jared, Priya, Mark. Carlos here. I'll mostly handle the technical questions.
[00:14] Jared: thanks, Sofia. we appreciate you taking the time. Quick context — AeroFin runs ML models for risk scoring and customer communications. We're shipping new generative features in mobile and web products, and latency is a big deal.
[00:27] Priya: yeah and infra-wise we currently run models on EC2 GPU instances in our VPC, but cost is ballooning, and our security team wants isolation and control over keys.
[00:37] Mark: timeline — pilot in next 4–6 weeks, production by Q2 end if everything looks good.
[00:44] Sofia: great. The purpose today is to see whether Redwood Dedicated fits — reserved GPUs for isolation/predictability — versus Hosted or Private. We'll go through throughput, burst strategy, scaling expectations, and any security must-haves.
[00:57] Carlos: quick note on terms: when I say "dedicated" I mean reserved GPU pools we provision for you — single-tenant capacity — whereas "hosted" is our multi-tenant API. "private" would be VPC or on-prem but with customer-managed control plane.
[01:10] Jared: perfect. So our rough workload: mostly short dialogues for customer messages, median request size ~60 tokens, peaks during market open which can be 10x baseline. We care about 95th p99 latency, p95 should be under 150ms for small prompts, p99 under 400ms ideally.
[01:30] Carlos: that's helpful. For Dedicated, we typically size for baseline throughput and then support bursts via a configured burst pool or autoscale to a higher tier. You can either commit to a larger reserved pool or allow burst capacity that bills at a higher rate.
[01:43] Priya: can you explain how burst works — is it instant? Are we talking pre-warm or spin-up times?
[01:50] Carlos: good question. Burst is typically a combination: we keep a small warm buffer of GPU workers for fast spikes; for larger sustained bursts we spin up additional instances — that can take a couple minutes depending on region and instance. We also do a lot of work with KV cache — kv cash in the transcript, sorry — key-value cache — to reduce repeated compute. For very latency-sensitive paths we recommend prefilling cache or active-prefix caching.
[02:19] Jared: okay so for market open spikes if it's a short 5–10 minute blip, the warm buffer would handle it?
[02:25] Carlos: yes, that's the idea. You can configure a buffer to cover expected transient spikes. If spikes exceed the buffer and are sustained, autoscale kicks in.
[02:34] Mark: what about single-tenant isolation — our security team says we need no co-tenancy on GPUs that can access specific data. Is that what Dedicated provides?
[02:41] Sofia: yes. Dedicated gives you isolated GPU pools and data isolation controls. For extra assurance you can choose Private where the control plane sits in your VPC or on-prem. But Dedicated means the actual inference workers are provisioned only for your account.
[02:54] Priya: and network connectivity — can Dedicated sit in our VPC or do we have to go through public endpoints?
[02:59] Carlos: with Dedicated we support VPC peering and private link setups in most regions — so low-latency network paths into your VPC. For fully customer-managed networking and air-gap requirements we'd look at Private.
[03:12] Jared: what's the SLA on latency and uptime for Dedicated?
[03:16] Sofia: we have SLA-backed uptime options for Dedicated. For latency, we publish performance profiles per model and hardware. We don't guarantee absolute p99 latency in the SLA today — it's more uptime and throughput — but we work with customers on performance SLOs as part of the contract.
[03:31] Mark: okay. And how do you handle model version pinning and rollouts? We need to be able to do canary rollouts and quick rollback.
[03:39] Carlos: you can pin model versions per route, do canary deployments, A/B tests, and set automatic fallback policies to compatible smaller model variants if capacity is constrained.
[03:50] Priya: what about encryption and KMS? Our security team mandates CMEK for keys and hardware HSM integrations.
[03:57] Carlos: we integrate with customer KMS in Private deployments; for Dedicated we support BYOK/KMS integrations via our key management hooks — we can discuss HSM specifics with security. Also we surface audit logs and per-request telemetry in the Console.
[04:10] Jared: how about cost — you mentioned committed reserved capacity vs burst billing. Can you give ballpark numbers for 1x A100 equivalent?
[04:19] Sofia: I'll send detailed pricing, but ballpark: reserved is discounted compared to on-demand; burst/overage is billed at a higher rate. I'll follow up with actual tiers — daily/hourly examples — as part of the pricing doc.
[04:30] Mark: do you support mixed GPU types in a pool — say we want a mix of A100 and cheaper T4-style nodes for background low-priority workloads?
[04:39] Carlos: yes, you can create pool tiers with different hardware profiles. We recommend mapping latency-sensitive routes to higher-tier GPUs and cheaper nodes to async or batch jobs. Routing policies can be latency-first or cost-first.
[04:52] Priya: for scaling, what's the unit of scale? Can you add one GPU at a time or are we provisioning in chunks?
[04:59] Carlos: we generally provision in worker instances; depending on provider and instance type you might scale by instance (e.g., 8-GPU instance) or by single-GPU VMs. We can design a configuration to give you finer-grained scale increments if needed. We'll detail that in the PoC plan.
[05:13] Jared: on the benchmarking side — we'll want to run both throughput (tokens/sec) and p99 latency under representative load, including cold-starts. Can Redwood help run those benchmarks in our VPC?
[05:24] Carlos: absolutely — we'll run the tests from within the same network region and offer scripts. For Private deployments we can run on-prem benchmarks. For Dedicated we'll provision test workers inside your reserved pool.
[05:35] Priya: curious about observability — we need token-level cost breakdowns and per-route latency histograms.
[05:42] Sofia: Redwood Console gives token-level cost, per-route/model dashboards, traces, and error analysis. We can also add custom tracing hooks if you run distributed traces.
[05:51] Mark: what if we want to start small and then commit to a larger reserved pool later after PoC?
[05:56] Sofia: that's common. You can start with a small reserved commitment and allow burst/overage while evaluating. If you commit to a larger pool, we offer credit/discounts against prior usage during the contract term depending on the commitment.
[06:09] Jared: any paper trail for compliance? We'll need SOC 2, ISO27001 artifacts.
[06:14] Sofia: we have SOC2 Type II and ISO artifacts; Carlos will share the security pack. For Private deployments we can support additional audit integration.
[06:22] Priya: one last networking Q — do you need inbound open ports on our side or is it outbound only from our app to Redwood endpoints?
[06:29] Carlos: typically it's outbound from your side to our endpoints or via private link. For Private deployments we may need some inbound connectivity for the control plane depending on architecture, but we can detail exact firewall rules in the design doc.
[06:42] Jared: ok thanks. let's talk about metrics for success — for us the main success criteria: cost per 1M tokens <= our current baseline, p95 latency < 150ms for small prompts, and ability to keep data in our control.
[06:57] Sofia: that helps — we'll align the PoC to measure those metrics.
[07:03] Mark: do you support RBAC and SAML SSO for access to the console?
[07:07] Carlos: yes SSO via SAML/OIDC, RBAC, and audit logs are available.
[07:12] Priya: are there any gotchas with data retention? e.g., do logs or traces contain raw prompts?
[07:18] Sofia: by default we store request logs to help with debugging, but for Dedicated and Private you can configure retention and choose to disable storage of raw prompts. We'll surface options in security docs.
[07:31] Jared: on the technical side — model quantization and latency tradeoffs — do you help recommend quantization profiles per workload?
[07:38] Carlos: yes, Redwood Optimize will give suggestions on quantization and batching configuration. For Dedicated we'll propose model+quantization pairs that balance cost and quality for your prompt mix.
[07:49] Mark: do you support on-the-fly fallbacks to smaller model variants if capacity is constrained?
[07:55] Carlos: yep automatic fallback policies can route to compatible smaller variants to keep requests alive. You can configure quality thresholds.
[08:02] Priya: any requirements from our side to enable autoscaling? Do we need to provide metrics?
[08:07] Carlos: autoscaling is handled by the platform based on request queues and resource utilization. You can also hook custom metrics or thresholds if you want more control.
[08:15] Jared: let's get into a hypothetical sizing: our baseline 100 qps with bursts to 1k qps for 10 minutes; median 60 tokens, average tokens per request 120 — what does that look like?
[08:28] Carlos: rough calc: tokens/sec at baseline ~ (100 qps * 120 tokens) = 12k tokens/sec; at peak 120k tokens/sec. Depending on model and GPU model, that could map to N GPUs; we'll model it in the benchmark spreadsheet. For small generative responses the per-token throughput matters a lot.
[08:44] Jared: ok makes sense. We should probably test 4, 8, and 16 GPU pools as you suggested.
[08:50] Sofia: noted — Carlos will propose those configs.
[08:55] Mark: curious about versioning — if we pin a model and want to roll a change, can that be done without reprovisioning the whole pool?
[09:02] Carlos: yes you can roll the model on the fleet gradually. The runtime supports rolling restarts without full reprovisioning in many cases, depending on architecture.
[09:10] Priya: anything special for GPU drivers and CUDA compatibility? We maintain a strict stack for some in-house tech.
[09:16] Carlos: we manage driver/kernel versions; if you have strict requirements we can support custom images in Private or Dedicated with advance planning.
[09:25] Jared: what about logs and PII — we're sending customer messages; we need to ensure PII isn't stored.
[09:31] Sofia: you can set retention and disable storage of raw prompts; we also offer field-level redaction options and tokenization hooks. We'll include that in the security pack.
[09:46] Carlos: quick small note — sometimes transcripts show product names wrong — we call the caching prefix KV cache and we've seen it transcribed as KV cash in other notes, haha.
[09:55] Priya: (laughs) noted.
[10:00] Sofia: circling back to procurement — Mark, do you have any procurement constraints or preferred contract terms?
[10:06] Mark: we prefer annual commitments with ramp; payment via ACH, standard net-45 is okay. Need one to two week lead time for legal review.
[10:13] Sofia: that works. We'll surface standard enterprise T&C and start a redline doc after pricing is agreed.
[10:19] Jared: are there any partner or reseller routes — we use a cloud reseller for credits sometimes.
[10:25] Sofia: yes we can work through marketplace or reseller channels if needed.
[10:29] Priya: okay last item — do you have a recommended template for benchmark payloads? We'd prefer not to reinvent it.
[10:35] Carlos: yes, we'll share a benchmark template with representative traces and scripts. I'll include guidance for cold starts, steady-state, and burst patterns.
[10:44] Mark: great. Let's recap next steps.
[10:47] Sofia: recap: we'll send pricing, security pack, and benchmark plan. We'll schedule a PoC kickoff for provisioning reserved GPUs and run 4/8/16 GPU tests. AeroFin will share sample payloads, latency targets, and networking constraints.
[11:00] Jared: yep, we'll get docs over. Thanks.
[11:03] Sofia: thanks everyone. We'll follow up with calendar invites for the PoC.
[11:07] meeting end
